newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS--Horlick pleads case on trip to Frankfurt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Horlick pleads case on trip to Frankfurt.

text.p: Defiant fund manager Nicola Horlick took an impromptu trip to Frankfurt on Friday to confront the management of Deutsche Bank, saying she wanted her job back and charging she was suspended from the bank's London subsidiary on the basis of hearsay.

"There has been a very large misunderstanding. They should have asked me, they decided to suspend me on the basis of hearsay," said the former head of pension fund business at London-based Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM).

The fund manager, 35, was suspended earlier this week pending the outcome of an internal investigation into what Deutsche Morgan Grenfell described as "a potential breach of her contract." She resigned on Thursday.

After a two-hour meeting with a Deutsche Bank personnel official and a lawyer for the bank, which yielded no decision on her future, Horlick said she would seek an unspecified amount of compensation if she was not reinstated.
The dispute with MGAM is believed to revolve around allegations that Horlick tried to take a number of her MGAM team with her in a move to Dutch Bank ABN AMRO.

Visibly angry at the way she said she had been treated by MGAM, Horlick described herself as "one individual against a huge organisation" and said: "That is appalling. I am sorry, I am not going to be treated like this."
But she later struck a conciliatory tone on her way back to the airport, telling Reuters she had been given "a fair hearing" at the bank's twin-towered headquarters in Frankfurt.

Although she failed to meet management board members, Horlick said she was "really impressed" by the attitude of the officials she met. No formal agreement was reached at the meeting, but Horlick said Deutsche would now examine the allegations against her.

But relations with MGAM took a turn for the worse just before she was due to board her flight when MGAM said Deutsche had only met her out of courtesy and that all matters related to her former employment had to be addressed to her former employers -- MGAM.

Asked by a Reuter reporter at Frankfurt airport how she reacted to MGAM's latest statement, Horlick said: "If Deutsche Morgan Grenfell is now saying these talks were irrelevant then naturally I am very upset and want clarification."

During her visit Horlick seemed happy to answer reporters' questions and pose for photographers from British newspapers who had accompanied her on her flight before marching up to the reception, surrounded by reporters.
She herself informed British TV crews of her plans after spending the morning on a fruitless quest to speak with senior MGAM officials at the company's London headquarters.
Horlicks said she felt vindicated by her visit to the trading floor at MGAM, during which, she said, she loudly proclaimed "Justice will be done", prompting some smiles from her erstwhile colleagues.
The furore had its roots in what she called "the Peter Young affair", referring to the MGAM crisis last year involving miscalculations at three of MGAM's European funds.
Horlick said she had been approached by many other institutions offering her new positions since her departure from MGAM.
Asked about allegations she had been planning to defect to ABN Amro, she said: "ABN Amro have refuted that and I concur with that. I was never planning a team move.
"With a child in chemotherapy for leukaemia I am not really in a position to start a new business," said the mother of five. She said she never thought she would be unemployed.
Horlick said she was planning to take legal action against her former employer over what she called her "constructive dismissal" by the investment bank.
